title: The Vets
strapline: A poorly puppy, a worried owner and a very gentle vet — kindness with a stethoscope.
intent: Caring for animal patients gives children a powerful reason to be gentle — soft hands, quiet voices, careful examinations.
The vets doubles the empathy of the doctors: there's a poorly pet to make better and a worried owner to reassure.
Children draw on and deepen what they know about real animals — what they eat, how they move, what they need to be well.
Specific vocabulary flourishes: paw, whiskers, kennel, hutch, injection, medicine, check-up, microchip.
Appointment books, patient record cards and medicine labels give writing a job at every desk.
Weighing, measuring and comparing patients — the heavy rabbit, the tiny hamster — slips real maths into the surgery.
implementation: Arrive as a worried owner with a poorly pet and a vague story — let the vet ask the questions and find the problem.
Model gentle handling constantly and explicitly: 'I'm holding him softly so he isn't frightened — can you listen to his heart?'
Feed in animal knowledge as genuine wondering: 'What do rabbits eat? Where does a tortoise sleep? How can we tell she's feeling better?'
Set up patient record cards — name, animal, what's wrong, what will help — and fill them in together at first.
Add a balance scale and tape measure so every patient gets weighed and measured at check-in.
Link to real animal care in the setting — feeding the fish, watering the plants — so gentleness travels beyond the play.
Follow real events: a child's new kitten or a pet's trip to the actual vet is tomorrow's richest storyline.
key_questions: What's brought you in today — what have you noticed about your pet?
How should we hold her so she feels safe?
What does this animal need every day to stay healthy?
Which patient is heavier — how could we find out?
How will the owner know what to do when they get home?

impact.text: Children replay vet scenes — check-ups, bandaged paws, medicine spoons — and grow them into full surgery storylines with waiting room, examinations and rules.
Children handle the animal patients gently as a matter of course, and remind friends to do the same.
Children use and explain new animal and medical vocabulary — whiskers, hutch, injection, check-up, microchip.
Children ask real questions about real animals — what they eat, where they sleep, why they hide — and expect proper answers.
Children 'write' patient records, appointment cards and medicine labels, and read them back to anxious owners.
Children comfort the worried owner as carefully as the poorly pet — 'don't worry, she'll be better soon'.
Children weigh and measure their patients, comparing who's heavier, longer or smallest, and count out 'one spoon of medicine a day'.
Children wrap bandages round little legs and fasten pet carriers with careful, controlled hands.

enhancements: A basket of soft-toy patients of honestly different sizes — hamster to Great Dane — for weighing and comparing.
Bandages, cotton wool, syringes (needle-free) and empty medicine boxes with labels to write.
Patient record cards and an appointment book at the reception desk.
A balance scale and tape measure at the check-in table.
Pet carriers, baskets and a 'recovery ward' of boxes with blankets.
Non-fiction animal books beside the waiting room chairs for diagnosis research.
A visit from a real (calm) pet with its owner, or a walk past the local vets' window.

playing_exploring: Children pour what they know and feel about animals into a world where they're the expert in the white coat.
Soft-toy patients are safe to practise on — brave enough for any injection.
active_learning: A patient admitted must be examined, treated and sent home well: children hold the whole care story and see it through.
creating_thinking: Children reason about causes and cures — he's limping, so let's look at his paw — and invent treatments, wards and recovery plans of their own.
